name: Hypoallergenic bedding / dust mite control

card.summary: Allergen-proof bedding to limit mites; useful for dust allergy, untested for facial puffiness.

quick.overview:
Mite-proof covers and hot washing reduce dust mite allergens.

Some link allergies to a puffy morning face, but no study tests bedding for appearance.
quick.mechanism: Covers and washing limit contact with mite allergens that trigger rhinitis and eye symptoms.
quick.risks: Low risk. Sources note partial covers need regular cleaning.

lead: Hypoallergenic bedding and dust mite control means using allergen-proof covers, hot washing and humidity reduction to limit mite allergens in the bedroom. People in looksmaxxing and skin-care circles use it with the aim of waking up with less facial puffiness, calmer skin and clearer-looking eyes, since mite allergy can bring congestion, itchy or watery eyes and flare-ups of eczema [2][4].

House dust mites live in mattresses and bedding and feed on shed skin; surveys have detected mite allergen in about 84 percent of US beds [1]. Dust mite allergy is a common cause of allergic rhinitis and asthma, and mite exposure is believed to contribute to atopic dermatitis [2][4]. Allergic rhinitis can pool blood in the veins beneath the eyes, producing dark under-eye patches known as allergic shiners [5].

Standard measures include fully enclosing mattress, pillows and duvet in mite-proof covers, weekly hot washing and keeping indoor humidity below about 50 percent [1][2]. Studies of these measures have mostly looked at asthma, and no study has tested bedding changes for facial appearance.

chain: Mite-proof covers, hot washing and lower humidity
Lower mite allergen exposure during sleep
Less congestion, eye itching and eczema flaring, so a less puffy, calmer-looking face
angle.text: For people who are allergic to dust mites, reducing exposure in the bed is meant to lessen nasal congestion, watery eyes and skin flares that show on the face in the morning, including dark under-eye patches linked to allergic rhinitis.

paras: House dust mites are about 0.2-0.3 mm long and accumulate in mattresses and bedding [1]. Allergy symptoms include sneezing, congestion, and itchy or watery eyes [2].

Wikipedia reports that exposure to dust mites is believed to contribute to the risk of atopic dermatitis and that mites are among common things that worsen it. Atopic dermatitis commonly affects the eyelids, where swelling can create an extra crease under the eye called a Dennie-Morgan fold [4]. Allergic shiners, dark patches under the eyes often seen with those folds, result from blood pooling in veins beneath the eyes because of nasal congestion from allergic rhinitis, and can continue into adulthood if the allergy is not addressed [5].

Suggested measures include fully enclosing mattress, pillows and duvet in mite-proof covers, weekly bedding changes, hot washing and keeping indoor humidity below about 50 percent [1][2]. One source notes that attempts to remove mites completely have not been shown to work well [2]. A review of textiles in atopic dermatitis also discusses fabric choice, noting that natural fibres such as cotton are preferred and wool can irritate atopic skin [6].

Cochrane reviews of mite control for people with mite-sensitive asthma, which included 54 trials with 3,002 patients in the 2008 update, reported that many trials were of poor quality and did not find an effect on asthma outcomes; 26 trials of the physical methods tested mattress encasings [3][7]. A Lancet editorial in 2008 was titled around the conclusion that mite control measures were of no use for asthma [8]. These reviews address asthma, not facial appearance, and proponents of allergen-proof covers generally focus on allergic rhinitis and eczema symptoms, for which such trials are separate.

No studies found on bedding or mite control and facial appearance. Randomised trials and meta-analyses of mite control measures in mite-sensitive asthma exist, including a 1998 BMJ meta-analysis and several Cochrane reviews [3][7][9]. Allergen immunotherapy is the main treatment described for mite allergy [2].
